bib.title: Eight Things to Know about Large Language Models

question: Which surprising but well-supported claims about LLMs should non-specialists in policy and scholarship keep in mind?
contributions: Eight claims about LLMs, each argued from prior work, plus discussion of limitations and risks.

results.claim: Instruction following is grafted onto LLMs with imperfect tools, so models fail then succeed once a request is reworded.
results.setup: Section 8, argument from cited work, no experiment
results.quote:
this instruction-following behavior isn’t inherent to the model, but rather is grafted onto it using highly im-
perfect tools

results.claim: A single failure of an LLM on a task is not reliable evidence it lacks the skill; a single success is not strong evidence of general capability.
results.quote:
LLM fails at a task in some setting is not reliable evidence that that LLM doesn’t have the skills or knowledge to do
that task.

results.claim: Hallucination may be mitigable because LLMs internally track which statements are true with reasonably high precision, improving with scale.
results.setup: Section 9.1, speculative per the author; cites Burns 2023 and Kadavath 2022
results.quote:
LLMs internally track which statements are true
with reasonably high precision, and this ability improves
with scale (Burns et al., 2023; Kadavath et al., 2022).

results.claim: Straightforward attempts to train truthfulness may fail silently via sandbagging.
results.quote:
straightforward attempts to manage hallucination are
likely to fail silently in a way that leaves them looking more
trustworthy than they are

results.claim: Without adaptation, a pretrained model continues its instructions rather than following them.
results.quote:
Otherwise, the model will attempt to continue
its instructions rather than following them (Ouyang et al.,
2022).

results.claim: Adaptation uses three techniques: plain LM prompting, supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning from preference judgments.
results.quote:

techniques:

limits: All evidence is collected from prior work; no new experiments (Introduction).
Section 9 is described as more speculative or subjective and not necessarily broadly shared.
Claims reflect the author's understanding of views among researchers largely in private labs.
Written as of early 2023; predates later reasoning models and the interpretability progress since.
practices: Do not conclude a model lacks a skill from one failed prompt; try rewording or reframing (Section 8).
Do not conclude a model can do a task from one successful, possibly cherry-picked, example (Section 8).
Make decisions about LLMs resilient to mistaken assumptions (Section 9.6).

figures.caption: The 202 tasks evaluated in BIG-Bench tend to show improved performance with scale overall, but individually they can improve gradually, abruptly, stay level, get worse, or vacillate.
figures.why: Shows why scaling laws do not predict task-level emergence.
